definition: Entrenched means firmly established and difficult to change.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word entrenched. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know entrenched should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Tipping is so entrenched in American restaurants that every attempt to swap it for a service charge has quietly fizzled.
An accepted practice has merely won agreement; an entrenched one has dug in and repels attempts to change it.
Unshakable goes past entrenched — no argument, cost, or campaign will ever move it at all.

Ingrained habits are worked into the grain of a person or a culture by years of repetition — quiet, internal, second nature. Entrenched points outward: a practice that has dug defenses and beats back open attempts to change it. Ingrained explains why you keep doing it; entrenched explains why reformers keep failing.

Deep-rooted describes what long years have anchored far below the surface, like a tree grown down through decades. Entrenched adds the military picture: not only old or deep, but actively defended, so that campaigns against it break and fail. Deep-rooted measures age and depth; entrenched measures resistance.

Entrenched means firmly established and difficult to change.
The QWERTY keyboard was laid out in the 1870s, partly to keep a mechanical typewriter's arms from jamming.
The jamming arms are gone; the layout is not.
Provably faster arrangements have been designed, marketed, and forgotten for a century, because the cost of retraining every typist on earth defeats every argument.
QWERTY is entrenched — not best, just dug in.
Entrenched is the exact word because it names what is firmly established and difficult to change — a practice that has dug fortifications, so that challenges break against it.
The military picture is the point: entrenched things are not merely old or common; they are defended by habit, cost, and inertia.
You don't tidy an entrenched arrangement away.
You campaign against it, and usually lose.
Entrenched is the reporter's word for practices, beliefs, and interests that have dug in against change — use it when reform keeps failing.
This unit's conventionally describes the accepted way of doing things; a convention becomes entrenched precisely when attempts to change it start breaking against the habit.
For roots-and-character images, ingrained is the gentler cousin.

In 1975, Congress named the metric system the preferred standard for American trade and created a board to manage the changeover.
For a few years the effort seemed to move: some highway signs showed kilometers, weather reports gave temperatures both ways, and factories printed dual labels.
Then the board was dissolved, the signs came down, and the country went back to measuring in miles, gallons, and degrees Fahrenheit.
The old units are entrenched.
Every deed, recipe, and speed limit assumes them, and anyone who converts alone gains nothing until everyone else converts too.
Scientists and doctors work in metric behind the scenes, but at the grocery store and on the highway, the campaign that Congress itself endorsed made almost no lasting mark.
